The inflection point: embracing responsible artificial intelligence in medical education.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in medicine has substantially outpaced its formal integration into medical training programs. This editorial synthesizes the evidence on AI in medical education, examining rapid growth alongside thin long-term outcomes data and structural tensions across curriculum, assessment, and global equity. Technology dependence, institutional inequity, and the mismatch between AI-enabled training and AI-free board examinations emerge as under-addressed challenges. We propose a four-tier disclosure framework to standardize transparency in AI-assisted scholarship and argue that AI literacy now constitutes a core clinical competency. Governance scholarship must match the pace of capability research if the field is to advance responsibly.

articles.title: Comparison of emergency department-measured optic nerve sheath diameter according to early neurological outcome in pediatric patients with traumatic brain injury.
articles.abstract: Early risk stratification in pediatric traumatic brain injury (TBI) is challenging, and readily available bedside markers may help identify children at risk of an adverse clinical course. This study compared emergency department (ED)-measured optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) and related ocular ultrasound measurements according to early neurological outcome in children with TBI. This perspective observational study was conducted at Mardani-Azar Pediatric Medical Center, Tabriz, Iran, between January and December 2025. Children younger than 18 years with TBI underwent ocular ultrasonography during their ED evaluation. Bilateral ONSD, eyeball transverse diameter (ETD), and interocular distance (IOD) were measured, and the ONSD/ETD and ONSD/IOD ratios were calculated. Neurological status was assessed 3-5 days after admission using the Glasgow coma scale (GCS). Associations between ultrasound measurements and early clinical outcomes were evaluated using between-group comparisons and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Among 100 patients, 84 patients (84%) had no CT findings suggestive of raised ICP, whereas 16 patients (16%) had at least one such finding. Mean ONSD was higher in the unfavorable-outcome group than in the favorable-outcome group (5.84 ± 0.67 vs. 4.55 ± 0.41 mm; P < 0.001). The ONSD/ETD and ONSD/IOD ratios were also higher in the unfavorable-outcome group (both P < 0.001), whereas ETD and IOD did not differ significantly. Mean ONSD showed an area under the ROC curve of 0.961 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.913-0.994) for discriminating the study-defined outcome groups. ED-measured ONSD was associated with early neurological status in this pediatric TBI cohort. These findings suggest that ONSD may warrant further evaluation as an adjunctive bedside risk-stratification marker. Prospective validation using standardized outcome definitions and appropriate adjustment for initial injury severity is needed before its independent prognostic value can be established. Not applicable.

articles.title: Unified Command in Local Public Health: Case Studies of Rabies and Tuberculosis Responses in Douglas County, Nebraska.
articles.abstract: As public health emergencies become more frequent and complex, local health departments must increasingly rely on public-private partnerships and whole-community approaches to respond effectively. The Douglas County Health Department (DCHD), serving Nebraska's most populous county, demonstrates how a local agency can coordinate large-scale responses by implementing a unified command structure with diverse partners. This case study presents 2 concurrent public health emergencies that occurred in late 2023: (1) the detection of raccoon rabies virus variant (RRVV) in a domestic kitten, a pathogen not previously identified in Nebraska, and (2) the largest pediatric tuberculosis (TB) exposure investigated in the county's history. Both incidents required rapid coordination across local, state, and federal agencies, as well as engagement with healthcare systems and community organizations. In each response, DCHD activated a unified command structure to facilitate operational objectives, allocate resources, and coordinate risk communication. The rabies response included enhanced animal surveillance, a trap-vaccinate-release campaign, and the manual distribution of 18,000 oral rabies vaccine baits. No additional human or animal cases of RRVV were identified. The TB response involved identifying 643 exposed individuals, conducting mass testing clinics with local healthcare partners, and rapidly initiating prophylaxis for vulnerable populations. No cases of secondary transmission were identified. These case studies demonstrate how local health departments can lead complex responses by leveraging established partnerships, aligning with National Incident Management System principles, and coordinating unified command operations. Lessons learned from Douglas County's experience offer practical guidance for other jurisdictions preparing for zoonotic and airborne infectious disease threats, especially when internal resources are limited.
